RFD: Rules
First Read: 26-Feb-26
Enrolled, An Act,
SJR___ CELEBRATING THE LIFE AND MOURNING THE DEATH OF JO ANN
BLACKMON BLAND.
WHEREAS, with an overwhelming sense of loss, we mourn
the death, yet celebrate the life, of Mrs. Jo Ann Blackmon
Bland of Selma, Alabama, whose passing on February 19, 2026,
has left a void in the lives of her family and friends; and
WHEREAS, born on July 29, 1953, to Alfred Charles
Blackmon and Ludie Wright Blackmon, and lovingly raised by
her grandmother Sylvia Johnson, Mrs. Bland's early life was
shaped by faith, discipline, and resilience in the face of
segregation and injustice; and
WHEREAS, Mrs. Bland became involved in the Civil
Rights Movement as a child, attending meetings of the Dallas
County Voters League with her grandmother and later joining
the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, demonstrating
extraordinary courage and conviction at a young age; and
WHEREAS, by the age of 11 she had endured numerous
arrests for her participation in nonviolent demonstrations,
reflecting a remarkable commitment to justice and equality
rarely seen in one so young; and
WHEREAS, in 1965 she marched across the Edmund Pettus
Bridge on Bloody Sunday alongside hundreds of peaceful
demonstrators, an event that helped awaken the conscience of
the nation and contributed to the passage of the Voting
Rights Act of 1965; and
WHEREAS, Mrs. Bland was among the first students to
integrate A.G. Parrish High School in Selma, further
advancing the cause of equal access to education in her
community; and
WHEREAS, she later earned a degree from the College
of Staten Island and honorably served in the United States
Army, continuing her life of public service; and
WHEREAS, upon returning home to Selma, she co-founded
the National Voting Rights Museum and Institute and later
established Journeys for the Soul, through which she
educated visitors from around the world on the true history
and legacy of the Civil Rights Movement; and
WHEREAS, Mrs. Bland remained committed to preserving
the memory of the movement's everyday participants, working
to develop Foot Soldiers Park as a tribute to those whose
courage shaped American democracy; and
WHEREAS, throughout her life she reminded others that
the struggle for civil rights is not solely the story of one
people, but the shared history of the nation, and she
dedicated herself to ensuring that future generations would
understand both the sacrifices made and the progress
achieved; and
WHEREAS, beyond her public contributions, she was a
devoted mother, grandmother, mentor, and matriarch who
instilled in her family and community the values of faith,
discipline, integrity, and service; and
WHEREAS, she was preceded in death by her parents;
grandmother, Sylvia Johnson; sisters, Jackie Maxey and Lynda
Lowery; and brother, Al Blackmon; and
WHEREAS, left to cherish her memory are her son,
Antonio Bowie, Sr.; granddaughter, Jasmyn Bowie; grandsons,
Antonio Bowie, Jr., Samuel Bowie, and Jordan Bowie; sisters,
Sadie Moss, Mary Myles, and Mary Hudson; and a host of
nieces, nephews, cousins, extended family members, and
lifelong friends; and
WHEREAS, Mrs. Bland's life stands as a testament to
courage rooted in faith, and her legacy will continue
through those she taught, inspired, and guided; she will be
sorrowfully missed, but the memory of her good deeds
remains, and she will be forever treasured in the hearts of
those whose lives she shared; now therefore,
BE IT RESOLVED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF ALABAMA, BOTH
HOUSES THEREOF CONCURRING, That while mourning the death of
Mrs. Jo Ann Blackmon Bland, it is comforting to remember her
extraordinary life of courage, service, and devotion to the
principles of justice and equality, and this resolution is
offered to her grieving family with heartfelt sympathy.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, That "I, Senator Robert
Stewart, Jr., am deeply saddened to learn of the passing of
Jo Ann Bland: civil rights activist, economic development
champion, and visionary leader. I knew her as Momma Bland.
As a boy, I sat at her feet at the National Voting Rights
Museum while she served as curator, listening to stories
that shaped my understanding of courage and sacrifice.
Little did I know that years later she would become
my boss at Foot Soldiers Park. She lead downtown Selma
revitalization. Life has a way of bringing things full
circle.
She poured into generations with truth, strength, and
unwavering love for Selma. Her legacy is woven into the soil
of this sacred city.
I am praying for our Selma family and for our
community at large. Grateful beyond words that we were
blessed to know such a beautiful soul."
